title: Ezekiel 17:11–21
context: The LORD explains the riddle to the rebellious house. The king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, took its king and princes to Babylon, and made a covenant under oath with one of the royal offspring, so that the kingdom would stand by keeping it. That king rebelled by sending to Egypt for horses and troops. The LORD declares that he will die in Babylon, that Pharaoh will not help him, and that the broken oath is the LORD’s own oath, which he will bring on the king’s head. Readers commonly identify the deported king as Jehoiachin and the rebel as Zedekiah, in line with 2 Kings 24:12-20 and 2 Chronicles 36:10-13. Those accounts and Ezekiel 12:13 can be read alongside this passage without merging their details.

verses.text: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Moreover the LORD’s word came to me, saying, Arminian readers note that the LORD now explains what the hearers might not grasp, showing patience toward a rebellious house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the interpretation as part of the same revelation. The LORD both sets the riddle and supplies its meaning, so that the message cannot be dismissed as obscure.

verses.text: “Say now to the rebellious house, ‘Don’t you know what these things mean?’ Tell them, ‘Behold, the king of Babylon came to Jerusalem, and took its king, and its princes, and brought them to him to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: Say now to the rebellious house, Arminian readers note the challenge, Don’t you know what these things mean? The question presses the hearers to recognize events they had already witnessed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the first eagle is here plainly the king of Babylon, who took Jerusalem’s king and princes. The interpretation is given by the text itself and needs no speculation.

verses.text: He took one of the royal offspring, and made a covenant with him. He also brought him under an oath, and took away the mighty of the land,
verses.arminianNotes: He took one of the royal offspring, and made a covenant with him. Arminian readers see a real agreement freely entered under oath, which bound the king to keep his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare 2 Chronicles 36:13, which says Nebuchadnezzar had made him swear by God. The two accounts can be read side by side, each in its own setting, without merging them.

verses.text: that the kingdom might be brought low, that it might not lift itself up, but that by keeping his covenant it might stand.
verses.arminianNotes: that the kingdom might be brought low, that it might not lift itself up, Arminian readers note that the covenant offered a way to stand, if the king kept it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the arrangement was humbling yet protective. Keeping the covenant meant survival, while the following verse shows the course the king actually took.

verses.text: But he rebelled against him in sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and many people. Will he prosper? Will he who does such things escape? Will he break the covenant, and still escape?
verses.arminianNotes: But he rebelled against him in sending his ambassadors into Egypt, Arminian readers see a deliberate choice to seek horses and troops from Egypt rather than keep his word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the triple question, ending, Will he break the covenant, and still escape? Compare 2 Kings 24:20 on Zedekiah’s rebellion and Jeremiah 37:5-7 on Pharaoh’s army.

verses.text: “ ‘As I live,’ says the Lord GOD, ‘surely in the place where the king dwells who made him king, whose oath he despised, and whose covenant he broke, even with him in the middle of Babylon he will die.
verses.arminianNotes: As I live,’ says the Lord GOD, Arminian readers see the LORD’s oath answering the king’s broken oath; he will die in Babylon, in the place of the king who made him king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 25:7 records Zedekiah being blinded and carried to Babylon, and Ezekiel 12:13 says he will not see Babylon though he will die there. These can be named without harmonizing.

verses.text: Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company won’t help him in the war, when they cast up mounds and build forts to cut off many persons.
verses.arminianNotes: Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company won’t help him in the war, Arminian readers see the futility of trusting in Egypt when the siege mounds and forts are raised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Jeremiah 37:7, where Pharaoh’s army returns to Egypt. Both prophets warn that reliance on Egypt will fail, each in his own words.

verses.text: For he has despised the oath by breaking the covenant; and behold, he had given his hand, and yet has done all these things. He won’t escape.
verses.arminianNotes: For he has despised the oath by breaking the covenant; Arminian readers note the phrase he had given his hand, a pledge freely made and then deliberately violated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the verse repeats the charge to make it unmistakable. Breaking a sworn covenant, even with a foreign king, is treated as a grave offense.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘As I live, I will surely bring on his own head my oath that he has despised and my covenant that he has broken.
verses.arminianNotes: Therefore the Lord GOD says: Arminian readers see the LORD claiming the oath as his own, my oath that he has despised, so that breaking faith with Babylon was also breaking faith with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that because the oath was sworn by God (2 Chronicles 36:13), the LORD holds the king accountable for it. Both traditions see oath-keeping as a matter of faithfulness to God.

verses.text: I will spread my net on him, and he will be taken in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon, and will enter into judgment with him there for his trespass that he has trespassed against me.
verses.arminianNotes: I will spread my net on him, and he will be taken in my snare. Arminian readers see the LORD acting in judgment through the events of the siege and capture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD calls the net his own while the Babylonians carry out the capture; see the Judges 9:23 box on God and hostile agents. Ezekiel 12:13 uses nearly the same words.

verses.text: All his fugitives in all his bands will fall by the sword, and those who remain will be scattered toward every wind. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken it.’
verses.arminianNotes: All his fugitives in all his bands will fall by the sword, Arminian readers see the judgment reaching the king’s followers, with survivors scattered toward every wind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the closing formula, Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken it. The fulfillment will show that the word came from the LORD.
